claim: Dlx5/6-Cre activity is restricted to forebrain structures including striatum, cortex, globus pallidus, basal forebrain, and reticular thalamic nucleus
source: Using mT/mG and Rosa26 LacZ Cre-reporter lines (Soriano, 1999; Muzumdar et al., 2007), we confirmed that Cre activity was restricted to forebrain structures (striatum, cortex, globus pallidus, basal forebrain, reticular thalamic nucleus), and included both direct and indirect pathway-projecting striatal neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using Cre-reporter lines shown in Figure 1A, and cites prior work establishing these reporter systems.

claim: TorsinA protein is essentially completely deleted from striatum in Dlx-CKO mice
source: TorsinA immunohistochemistry confirmed the essentially complete deletion of torsinA protein from striatum, partial deletion from cortex (reflecting loss from GABAergic interneurons), and sparing of the thalamus–with the exception of the inhibitory neurons of the reticular thalamic nucleus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating torsinA protein levels in different brain regions.

claim: TorsinA is partially deleted from cortex in Dlx-CKO mice, reflecting loss from GABAergic interneurons
source: TorsinA immunohistochemistry confirmed the essentially complete deletion of torsinA protein from striatum, partial deletion from cortex (reflecting loss from GABAergic interneurons), and sparing of the thalamus–with the exception of the inhibitory neurons of the reticular thalamic nucleus (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 1B and inference that cortical deletion reflects GABAergic interneuron loss based on Dlx5/6-Cre expression pattern.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice are born in the expected Mendelian ratio
source: Dlx5/6-Cre+;Tor1aflx/− mice (herein Dlx5/6 conditional KO 'Dlx-CKO') are born in the expected Mendelian ratio and are indistinguishable initially from littermate controls, including normal postnatal weight gain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observational finding from breeding experiments, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice exhibit normal postnatal weight gain
source: Dlx5/6-Cre+;Tor1aflx/− mice (herein Dlx5/6 conditional KO 'Dlx-CKO') are born in the expected Mendelian ratio and are indistinguishable initially from littermate controls, including normal postnatal weight gain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by weight measurements over time shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dlx-CKO mouse forebrain architecture appears normal based on Nissl staining
source: Nissl-stained brain sections of Dlx-CKO mice did not demonstrate gross or microscopic abnormalities of forebrain architecture, and immunostaining showed no evidence of reactive gliosis or neural injury (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by histological examination shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice show no evidence of reactive gliosis
source: Nissl-stained brain sections of Dlx-CKO mice did not demonstrate gross or microscopic abnormalities of forebrain architecture, and immunostaining showed no evidence of reactive gliosis or neural injury (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining for GFAP, s100β, and Iba-1 shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cortical thickness does not differ between Dlx-CKO and control mice across developmental timepoints
source: Cortical thickness: two-way ANOVA main effect of age F3,65 = 17.24; p < 0.0001, genotype F1,65 = 0.35; p = 0.55
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Striatal volume does not differ between Dlx-CKO and control mice across developmental timepoints
source: striatal volume: main effect of age F3,65 = 307.0; p < 0.0001; genotype F1,65 = 0.724; p = 0.39
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Neonatal Dlx-CKO mice exhibit normal motor behavior including negative geotaxis and forelimb suspension
source: The behavior of neonatal Dlx-CKO mice is normal. Negative geotaxis and forelimb suspension did not differ from littermate controls. Forelimb suspension: t-test t(92) = 0.753; p = 0.45).
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice develop severe forelimb and hindlimb clasping at postnatal day 15
source: Dlx-CKO mice develop severe forelimb and hindlimb clasping at P15 (Chi square test, Χ2 = 64.03; p < 0.0001), and a subset exhibits severe trunk twisting.
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: A subset of Dlx-CKO mice exhibit severe trunk twisting
source: Dlx-CKO mice develop severe forelimb and hindlimb clasping at P15 (Chi square test, Χ2 = 64.03; p < 0.0001), and a subset exhibits severe trunk twisting.
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Approximately 70% of Dlx-CKO mice develop severe abnormal twisting of the trunk
source: A subset of these mutants simultaneously developed severe abnormal twisting of the trunk (∼70% of mice; Figure 1H).
evidence: Quantitative observation from behavioral testing.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice develop an inability to hang from a wire grid at 1 month of age
source: Dlx-CKO mice develop an inability to hang from a wire grid at 1 month of age (two-way ANOVA; main effect of genotype F1,269 = 16.63; p < 0.0001, time F6,269 = 6.613; p < 0.0001; and interaction F6,269 = 2.285; p = 0.036).
evidence: Supported by grid hang test data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Motor learning remains intact in Dlx-CKO mice as demonstrated by the accelerating rotarod test
source: Motor learning remains intact, as demonstrated by the accelerating rotarod test (two-way ANOVA main effect of trial F9,324 = 38.27 p < 0.0001, genotype: F1,36 = 3.591; p = 0.066).
evidence: Supported by rotarod performance data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Scopolamine treatment significantly reduces limb clasping and twisting in Dlx-CKO mice
source: Scopolamine-treated animals exhibited significantly less limb clasping and twisting than saline-treated animals throughout the treatment period (Figure 2B; main effect of drug F1,141 = 36.17; p < 0.0001, Sidak's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing during drug treatment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The symptomatic improvement from scopolamine depends on the continued presence of the drug
source: The symptomatic improvement appeared to depend on the continued presence of scopolamine, as behavioral benefit disappeared following a 3-week washout period.
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing after drug washout shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Trihexyphenidyl (THP) significantly reduces clasping in Dlx-CKO mice
source: Similar to scopolamine, THP (5 mg/kg, i.p.) significantly reduced clasping, and this effect resolved following a 3 week washout (Figure 2C; Main effect of drug F1,82 = 46.69; p < 0.0001, Sidak's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: Supported by behavioral testing during THP treatment shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) expression is significantly reduced in Dlx-CKO striatum
source: Western blot analyses of microdissected striatum demonstrated a significant reduction in choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), but no significant alterations in glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67) or tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: GAD67 expression does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control striatum
source: Western blot analyses of microdissected striatum demonstrated a significant reduction in choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), but no significant alterations in glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67) or tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control striatum
source: Western blot analyses of microdissected striatum demonstrated a significant reduction in choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), but no significant alterations in glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67) or tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and quantification shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: TrkA expression is reduced by approximately 50% in Dlx-CKO striatum
source: Consistent with this possibility, the receptor tyrosine kinase TrkA, expressed specifically by striatal LCIs (Sobreviela et al., 1994), was reduced by approximately 50% (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A,C and citation to prior work establishing TrkA as an LCI marker.

claim: TrkA is expressed specifically by striatal large cholinergic interneurons
source: Consistent with this possibility, the receptor tyrosine kinase TrkA, expressed specifically by striatal LCIs (Sobreviela et al., 1994), was reduced by approximately 50% (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sobreviela et al., 1994.

claim: DARPP-32 expression does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control striatum
source: In contrast, expression of the medium spiny projection neuron (MSN) marker DARPP-32 did not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO mice and littermate controls (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A,D.

claim: Extracellular acetylcholine levels are significantly reduced (approximately 73% reduction) in Dlx-CKO dorsal striatum
source: Levels of extracellular acetylcholine (ACh) were significantly reduced in Dlx-CKO mice (∼73% reduction from control levels, performed in the presence of the acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor neostigmine; 1070 ± 231 nM in control [n = 6] vs 290 ± 33 nM in KO [n = 8]; t12 = 3.89; p = 0.0021; Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by in vivo microdialysis measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Basal extracellular concentrations of 16 other neurotransmitters and metabolites do not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control striatum
source: In contrast, the basal extracellular concentrations of 16 other neurotransmitters and metabolites did not differ significantly from controls in a separate microdialysis study (n = 7 per group; Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by comprehensive microdialysis measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Striatal acetylcholinesterase (AChE) activity is significantly reduced in Dlx-CKO mice
source: Consistent with the reduction of ACh, histochemical analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in striatal AChE activity, an effect that appeared most prominent in dorsolateral striatum (Figure 3G, assay controls in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by histochemical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The reduction in AChE activity appears most prominent in dorsolateral striatum
source: Consistent with the reduction of ACh, histochemical analysis demonstrated a significant reduction in striatal AChE activity, an effect that appeared most prominent in dorsolateral striatum (Figure 3G, assay controls in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by histochemical analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice exhibit a 40% reduction in the number of striatal ChAT-positive neurons at 10 weeks of age
source: Unbiased stereological quantification of striatal ChAT-positive neurons demonstrated 40% reduction in LCI number in Dlx-CKO compared to control mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by stereological cell counting data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Cholinergic cell loss in Dlx-CKO mice is non-uniform with a predilection for dorsolateral (motor) striatum
source: Cell loss was non-uniform, showing a clear predilection for dorsolateral (motor) striatum, and a rostro-caudal gradient of cell loss, with relative sparing of caudal regions.
evidence: Supported by regional cell density analysis shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Cell loss in Dlx-CKO striatum shows a rostro-caudal gradient with relative sparing of caudal regions
source: Cell loss was non-uniform, showing a clear predilection for dorsolateral (motor) striatum, and a rostro-caudal gradient of cell loss, with relative sparing of caudal regions.
evidence: Supported by regional cell density analysis shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Cell loss is roughly 6 times greater in dorsolateral compared to ventromedial striatum (57% vs 9% reduction)
source: Strikingly, cell loss was roughly 6 times greater in dorsolateral compared to ventromedial striatum (57% vs 9% reduction; Figure 4C,D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by quantitative regional analysis shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dlx-CKO striata contain 40-50% fewer VAChT-positive large cholinergic interneurons
source: To address the possibility that the striatal abnormality reflects ChAT downregulation, we used stereology to quantify an independent marker of LCIs, vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT). Dlx-CKO striata again appeared to contain 40–50% fewer VAChT+ LCIs (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification of VAChT-positive cells shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Dlx-CKO striata show approximately 40% reduction in the number of Nissl-stained neuron profiles ≥20 µm
source: Stereological quantification of the number of Nissl-stained neuron profiles ≧20 µm demonstrated a ∼40% reduction in Dlx-CKO compared to littermate controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification of large Nissl-stained cells shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cholinergic neurons are approximately twice as large as GABAergic striatal neurons
source: To fully exclude the potential confound of phenotypic marker down regulation, we took advantage of the fact that cholinergic neurons are the largest striatal neurons, being approximately twice as large as GABAergic striatal neurons (Kreitzer, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kreitzer, 2009.

claim: The number of small and medium sized Nissl-stained striatal cells (≤20 µm) does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control mice
source: LCIs are the only non-GABAergic neurons in the striatum, so we first quantified the number of small and medium sized Nissl-stained striatal cells (i.e., ≤20 µm), and found no significant difference in their numbers (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Large cholinergic interneurons are the only non-GABAergic neurons in the striatum
source: LCIs are the only non-GABAergic neurons in the striatum, so we first quantified the number of small and medium sized Nissl-stained striatal cells (i.e., ≤20 µm), and found no significant difference in their numbers (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about striatal cell types.

claim: The number of cortical parvalbumin-positive interneurons does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control mice
source: We found no significant abnormalities in the number of cortical or striatal fast-spiking (marked by parvalbumin; 'PV') or low-threshold spiking (marked by somatostatin; 'SST') interneurons (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The number of cortical somatostatin-positive interneurons does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control mice
source: We found no significant abnormalities in the number of cortical or striatal fast-spiking (marked by parvalbumin; 'PV') or low-threshold spiking (marked by somatostatin; 'SST') interneurons (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The number of striatal parvalbumin-positive interneurons does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control mice
source: We found no significant abnormalities in the number of cortical or striatal fast-spiking (marked by parvalbumin; 'PV') or low-threshold spiking (marked by somatostatin; 'SST') interneurons (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The number of striatal somatostatin-positive interneurons does not differ significantly between Dlx-CKO and control mice
source: We found no significant abnormalities in the number of cortical or striatal fast-spiking (marked by parvalbumin; 'PV') or low-threshold spiking (marked by somatostatin; 'SST') interneurons (Figure 4F,H).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The number of striatal medium spiny neurons (marked by DARPP-32) does not differ between 10 week-old Dlx-CKO and littermate striata
source: Similarly, the number of striatal MSNs, (marked by DARPP-32) did not differ between 10 week-old Dlx-CKO and littermate striata (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The number of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons is normal in Dlx-CKO mice
source: In contrast to striatal LCIs, there is a normal number of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Figure 4G), despite the fact that these neurons also express Cre recombinase (Sanchez-Ortiz et al., 2012) and lack torsinA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 4G and citation to prior work.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons express Cre recombinase in the Dlx5/6-Cre model
source: In contrast to striatal LCIs, there is a normal number of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Figure 4G), despite the fact that these neurons also express Cre recombinase (Sanchez-Ortiz et al., 2012) and lack torsinA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanchez-Ortiz et al., 2012.

claim: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons lack torsinA in Dlx-CKO mice
source: In contrast to striatal LCIs, there is a normal number of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (Figure 4G), despite the fact that these neurons also express Cre recombinase (Sanchez-Ortiz et al., 2012) and lack torsinA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: At postnatal day 7, there are normal numbers of ChAT-positive neurons in Dlx-CKO striatum
source: At P7, when motor function is normal (Figure 1G,I), there were normal numbers of ChAT+ neurons (Figure 5A), and normal levels of ChAT and TrkA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At postnatal day 7, ChAT and TrkA protein levels are normal in Dlx-CKO striatum
source: At P7, when motor function is normal (Figure 1G,I), there were normal numbers of ChAT+ neurons (Figure 5A), and normal levels of ChAT and TrkA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Progressive loss of ChAT-positive neurons occurs from 1 to 2 months of age in Dlx-CKO mice
source: Progressive loss of ChAT+ neurons occurred from 1 to 2 months of age, a time period partially overlapping with the onset of motor dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification at multiple timepoints shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The number of ChAT-positive neurons is not reduced further at 6 months of age in Dlx-CKO mice
source: Numbers of ChAT+ neurons were not reduced further at the 6-month time point (Figure 5A), a time when motor abnormalities similarly plateaued.
evidence: Supported by stereological quantification shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice exhibit significantly more ChAT-positive neurons co-expressing cleaved caspase-3 at postnatal days 12-14 and 24
source: While CC3+ and CC3/ChAT+ cell numbers did not differ between mutant and littermate control mice at postnatal day 10, Dlx-CKO mice exhibited significantly more CC3/ChAT+ co-localized cells at postnatal days 12–14 and 24 (Figure 5B), precisely the time that abnormal movements emerge.
evidence: Supported by quantification of co-labeled cells shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There are no differences in the overall number of non-ChAT-positive cleaved caspase-3 striatal cells between Dlx-CKO and control mice
source: There were no differences in the overall number of non-ChAT+ CC3 striatal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Surviving large cholinergic interneurons in Dlx-CKO mice exhibit significant cell soma hypertrophy
source: Surviving LCIs exhibited significant cell soma hypertrophy (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The cell size frequency histogram of large cholinergic interneurons shows a rightward shift in Dlx-CKO mice
source: The delayed time course of this phenotype following cell loss and rightward shift of the cell size frequency histogram (Figure 6B) support the likelihood that surviving neurons are becoming larger.
evidence: Supported by frequency histogram analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive, somatostatin-positive, and DARPP-32-positive neurons in striatum and cortex show no changes in soma size in Dlx-CKO mice
source: In contrast, PV+, SST+, or DARPP-32+ neurons in striatum and cortex showed no changes in soma size (Figure 6C,D)
evidence: Supported by cell size measurements shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Medium spiny neuron dendritic structure is normal in Dlx-CKO mice as assessed by Golgi-Cox staining and Sholl analysis
source: and MSN dendritic structure was normal, as assessed by Golgi-Cox staining and Sholl analysis (Figure 6E–H).
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 6E-H.

claim: Spontaneous firing rates of large cholinergic interneurons are similar between Dlx-CKO and control mice
source: Spontaneous firing rates and coefficients of variation were similar for LCIs between Dlx-CKO and controls in cell-attached patch clamp mode (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Cell capacitance measurements are significantly larger in Dlx-CKO large cholinergic interneurons than control
source: However, cell capacitance measurements were significantly larger in Dlx-CKO LCIs than control (Figure 7C) when recorded at a membrane potential of −70 mV with a K-gluconate based internal recording solution, or using a cesium-methanesulfonate internal solution (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Dlx-CKO large cholinergic interneurons display significantly more spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents than control
source: Dlx-CKO LCIs displayed significantly more spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) than control LCIs (Figure 7D,E) (p = 0.006).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and analysis shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The sIPSC/sEPSC ratio is significantly higher in Dlx-CKO large cholinergic interneurons
source: The sIPSC/sEPSC ratio was significantly higher in Dlx-CKO cells (Figure 7G) indicating that these cells receive abnormal synaptic input.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Depolarizing current pulses produce significantly fewer action potentials in large cholinergic interneurons from Dlx-CKO than control at 150-200 pA current intensities
source: Depolarizing current pulses (1 s duration, 25 pA increments) produced significantly fewer action potentials in LCIs from Dlx-CKO than control at 150–200 pA current intensities (Figure 7H,I; two-way ANOVA, interaction between current intensity and frequency of action potentials, p < 0.001).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and analysis shown in Figure 7H,I.

claim: Evoked EPSCs from Dlx-CKO large cholinergic interneurons are significantly larger than those of control at higher stimulation intensities
source: However, evoked EPSCs from Dlx-CKO LCIs were significantly larger than those of control LCIs (Figure 7J,K) at higher stimulation intensities (two-way ANOVA, interaction between current intensity and response amplitude, p < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and analysis shown in Figure 7J,K.

claim: A subpopulation of Dlx-CKO large cholinergic interneurons (3/12) display very large evoked responses (>150 pA at 0.06 mA) not observed in control
source: A subpopulation of Dlx-CKO LCIs displayed very large responses (>150 pA at 0.06 mA, 3/12) that were not observed in control LCIs.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Large cholinergic interneurons exhibiting large amplitude responses have significantly larger membrane capacitances than cells that do not
source: LCIs exhibiting large amplitude responses also had significantly larger membrane capacitances than cells that did not (134.8 ± 14.7 vs 97.0 ± 8.3 pF, p = 0.047)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: TrkA levels are significantly reduced (approximately 84% reduction) in DYT1 postmortem putamen
source: TrkA levels were significantly reduced in DYT1 putamen (Figure 8B; approximately 84% reduction).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of human postmortem tissue shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Normalized mean expression levels of VAChT are reduced by 66% in DYT1 putamen, but this difference does not reach statistical significance
source: Similarly, the normalized mean expression levels of VAChT and AChE were reduced by 66% and 50% respectively (Figure 8B,C), but these differences did not reach statistical significance, likely because of the large variability between control subjects for these markers.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: Normalized mean expression levels of AChE are reduced by 50% in DYT1 putamen, but this difference does not reach statistical significance
source: Similarly, the normalized mean expression levels of VAChT and AChE were reduced by 66% and 50% respectively (Figure 8B,C), but these differences did not reach statistical significance, likely because of the large variability between control subjects for these markers.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 8B,C.

claim: GAD67 levels are comparable between control and DYT1 dystonia subjects in postmortem putamen
source: GAD67 and TH levels were comparable between control and DYT1 dystonia subjects (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase levels are comparable between control and DYT1 dystonia subjects in postmortem putamen
source: GAD67 and TH levels were comparable between control and DYT1 dystonia subjects (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Striatal dysfunction plays an important role in dystonia
source: Striatal dysfunction plays an important role in dystonia, but the striatal cell types that contribute to abnormal movements are poorly defined.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The striatal cell types that contribute to abnormal movements in dystonia are poorly defined
source: Striatal dysfunction plays an important role in dystonia, but the striatal cell types that contribute to abnormal movements are poorly defined.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Primary dystonia is characterized by disabling involuntary twisting movements
source: Primary dystonia encompasses a group of sporadic and inherited disorders characterized by disabling involuntary twisting movements.
evidence: This is a clinical definition of primary dystonia.

claim: The sole clinical feature of primary dystonia implies selective abnormalities of motor pathways
source: This sole clinical feature of primary dystonia implies selective abnormalities of motor pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical presentation.

claim: Primary dystonia is widely accepted to result from abnormal functioning of a structurally intact central nervous system
source: The absence of an overt neuropathological signature complicates identification of pathogenic brain structures and cell types, and underlies the widely accepted notion that primary dystonia results from abnormal functioning of a structurally intact central nervous system (CNS).
evidence: This is stated as a widely accepted notion in the field.

claim: Secondary dystonia is linked strongly to striatal (especially putaminal) damage
source: Secondary dystonia–where symptoms result from CNS damage or exogenous pharmacological insult–is linked strongly to striatal (especially putaminal) damage (Marsden et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Marsden et al., 1985.

claim: Therapeutic benefit from antimuscarinic drugs implicates striatal dysfunction in dystonia
source: Therapeutic benefit from antimuscarinic drugs (Burke et al., 1986) also implicates striatal dysfunction, as striatal cholinergic interneurons play a poorly understood but important role in motor control.
evidence: Supported by citation to Burke et al., 1986 and inference about the role of striatal cholinergic interneurons.

claim: Striatal cholinergic interneurons play a poorly understood but important role in motor control
source: Therapeutic benefit from antimuscarinic drugs (Burke et al., 1986) also implicates striatal dysfunction, as striatal cholinergic interneurons play a poorly understood but important role in motor control.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Striatal-associated behavioral and functional imaging abnormalities are present in primary dystonia
source: Striatal-associated behavioral (Carbon et al., 2011) and functional imaging abnormalities are present in primary dystonia (reviewed in Pappas et al. (2014))
evidence: Supported by citations to Carbon et al., 2011 and review by Pappas et al., 2014.

claim: Altering basal ganglia output with deep brain stimulation therapy is an effective dystonia treatment
source: and altering basal ganglia output with deep brain stimulation therapy is an effective dystonia treatment (Vidailhet et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vidailhet et al., 2013.

claim: The key striatal cell type(s) that drive dystonic movements are unknown
source: Despite this evidence, the key striatal cell type(s) that drive dystonic movements are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: DYT1 dystonia is a neurodevelopmental disorder manifesting during childhood
source: Studies aimed at defining mechanistic features in primary dystonia primarily use rodent models of DYT1 dystonia, a neurodevelopmental disorder manifesting during childhood, and the most common inherited primary dystonia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DYT1 dystonia.

claim: DYT1 dystonia is the most common inherited primary dystonia
source: Studies aimed at defining mechanistic features in primary dystonia primarily use rodent models of DYT1 dystonia, a neurodevelopmental disorder manifesting during childhood, and the most common inherited primary dystonia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: DYT1 dystonia is caused by a dominantly inherited mutation of the TOR1A gene
source: DYT1 dystonia is caused by a dominantly inherited mutation of the TOR1A gene that impairs function of the encoded protein torsinA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the genetic basis of DYT1 dystonia.

claim: The DYT1 mutation impairs function of the encoded protein torsinA
source: DYT1 dystonia is caused by a dominantly inherited mutation of the TOR1A gene that impairs function of the encoded protein torsinA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: TorsinA is an endoplasmic reticulum/nuclear envelope-localized AAA+ ATPase
source: TorsinA is an endoplasmic reticulum/nuclear envelope-localized AAA+ ATPase (Ozelius et al., 1997) implicated in protein quality control and nuclear membrane-localized functions (reviewed in Dauer (2014)).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ozelius et al., 1997.

claim: TorsinA is implicated in protein quality control and nuclear membrane-localized functions
source: TorsinA is an endoplasmic reticulum/nuclear envelope-localized AAA+ ATPase (Ozelius et al., 1997) implicated in protein quality control and nuclear membrane-localized functions (reviewed in Dauer (2014)).
evidence: Supported by review citation to Dauer (2014).

claim: Heterozygous Tor1aΔE/+ mice do not exhibit any overt abnormalities
source: Heterozygous Tor1aΔE/+ mice (mimicking the human DYT1 genotype) do not exhibit any overt abnormalities, while constitutive Tor1a knockout and homozygous ΔE knock-in mice both exhibit perinatal lethality (Goodchild et al., 2005; Tanabe et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodchild et al., 2005 and Tanabe et al., 2012.

claim: Constitutive Tor1a knockout mice exhibit perinatal lethality
source: Heterozygous Tor1aΔE/+ mice (mimicking the human DYT1 genotype) do not exhibit any overt abnormalities, while constitutive Tor1a knockout and homozygous ΔE knock-in mice both exhibit perinatal lethality (Goodchild et al., 2005; Tanabe et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodchild et al., 2005 and Tanabe et al., 2012.

claim: Homozygous ΔE knock-in mice exhibit perinatal lethality
source: Heterozygous Tor1aΔE/+ mice (mimicking the human DYT1 genotype) do not exhibit any overt abnormalities, while constitutive Tor1a knockout and homozygous ΔE knock-in mice both exhibit perinatal lethality (Goodchild et al., 2005; Tanabe et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodchild et al., 2005 and Tanabe et al., 2012.

claim: Transgenic mice overexpressing wild type or mutant torsinA do not exhibit overt motor abnormalities
source: Transgenic mice overexpressing wild type or mutant torsinA do not exhibit overt motor abnormalities (Sharma et al., 2005), but are used to explore striatal electrophysiological abnormalities linked to overexpression of mutant torsinA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharma et al., 2005.

claim: In DYT1 mutant transgenics, striatal large cholinergic interneurons exhibit a paradoxical response to dopamine D2 receptor agonists
source: These studies demonstrate that in DYT1 mutant transgenics, striatal large cholinergic interneurons (LCI) exhibit a paradoxical response to dopamine D2 receptor agonists that may be involved in abnormalities of corticostriatal plasticity (Pisani et al., 2006; Martella et al., 2009; Sciamanna et al., 2011; Grundmann et al., 2012; Sciamanna et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Conditional deletion of torsinA in single brain regions or cell types causes subtle changes in motor function but no overt abnormal movements
source: Conditional deletion of torsinA in single brain regions (e.g., cortex, striatum) or cell types (e.g., cerebellar Purkinje cells, cholinergic neurons) implicated in the disease causes subtle changes in motor function, but no overt abnormal movements (Yokoi et al., 2008, 2011; Zhang et al., 2011; Sciamanna et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Overt twisting movements are only observed in DYT1 model mice where torsinA function is impaired in precursor cells giving rise to multiple neuronal cell types
source: Overt twisting movements are only observed in DYT1 model mice where torsinA function is impaired in precursor cells giving rise to multiple neuronal cell types (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2014.

claim: DYT1 model mice with overt twisting movements exhibit focal neurodegeneration in a discrete set of sensorimotor structures
source: These models exhibit focal neurodegeneration in a discrete set of sensorimotor structures, and together with human subject neuroimaging studies (reviewed in Ramdhani and Simonyan (2013)), raise questions regarding the 'normal structure, abnormal function' hypothesis of primary dystonias.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2014 (implied from context) and review citation.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice exhibit face, construct and predictive validity as a model of DYT1 dystonia
source: This model exhibits face, construct and predictive validity.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the multiple findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The onset of abnormal movements in Dlx-CKO mice coincides with selective loss of striatal large cholinergic interneurons
source: These mice are initially normal, but exhibit overt motor deficits as juveniles, coincident with selective loss of striatal LCIs and related electrophysiological abnormalities.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The abnormal twisting and clasping movements of Dlx-CKO mice are reduced significantly with chronic antimuscarinic administration
source: Similar to DYT1 patients, the abnormal twisting and clasping movements of these mice are reduced significantly with chronic antimuscarinic administration.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Dorsal large cholinergic interneurons have a unique requirement for torsinA function during striatal maturation
source: These findings demonstrate that dorsal LCI have a unique requirement for torsinA function during striatal maturation, and link abnormalities of these cells to dystonic-like movements in an overtly symptomatic animal model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented.

claim: Abnormalities of dorsal large cholinergic interneurons are linked to dystonic-like movements in Dlx-CKO mice
source: These findings demonstrate that dorsal LCI have a unique requirement for torsinA function during striatal maturation, and link abnormalities of these cells to dystonic-like movements in an overtly symptomatic animal model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, particularly the temporal correlation between LCI loss and movement onset, and the therapeutic response to antimuscarinics.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice are hyperactive in the open field
source: Dlx-CKO mice are also significantly hyperactive in the open field (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by open field activity data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dystonia in humans is commonly exacerbated by action
source: Dystonia in humans is commonly exacerbated by action, and may occur exclusively in particular settings or during specific motor tasks (e.g., runner's dystonia, dystonic writer's cramp).
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge about dystonia.

claim: Gait analysis of Dlx-CKO mice is largely unremarkable
source: Gait analysis was largely unremarkable (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by gait analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nearly 100% of Dlx-CKO mice develop severe forelimb and hindlimb clasping behaviors beginning at 15-17 days of age
source: Dlx-CKO mice exhibited normal behavior during tail suspension up to 14 days of age, but nearly 100% of the animals developed severe forelimb and hindlimb clasping behaviors beginning at 15–17 days of age (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral observations shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The abnormal clasping behavior in Dlx-CKO mice remains fixed for the duration of the animal's life to at least 1 year of age
source: This abnormal behavior remained fixed for the duration of the animal's life, to at least 1 year of age (17 out of 18 Dlx-CKO mice clasped during tail suspension at 1 year).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal behavioral observations.

claim: Chronic antimuscarinic administration is a common therapy for DYT1 dystonia
source: Chronic antimuscarinic administration is a common therapy for DYT1 dystonia (Burke et al., 1986)
evidence: Supported by citation to Burke et al., 1986.

claim: Trihexyphenidyl is the most commonly used antimuscarinic agent to treat DYT1 dystonia
source: The antimuscarinic trihexyphenidyl (THP) is the most commonly used agent to treat DYT1 dystonia and is clinically validated (Burke et al., 1986; Jankovic, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burke et al., 1986 and Jankovic, 2013.

claim: Trihexyphenidyl is clinically validated for treatment of DYT1 dystonia
source: The antimuscarinic trihexyphenidyl (THP) is the most commonly used agent to treat DYT1 dystonia and is clinically validated (Burke et al., 1986; Jankovic, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burke et al., 1986 and Jankovic, 2013.

claim: Antimuscarinics effectively reduce clasping and twisting behaviors in Dlx-CKO mice
source: These data indicate that antimuscarinics effectively reduce clasping and twisting behaviors, and support the predictive validity of Dlx-CKO mice for the study of DYT1 dystonia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The reduction in ChAT expression suggests a specific abnormality of cholinergic elements in Dlx-CKO striatum
source: Western blot analyses of microdissected striatum demonstrated a significant reduction in choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), but no significant alterations in glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD67) or tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression (Figure 3A,B), suggesting a specific abnormality of cholinergic elements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the selective reduction in cholinergic markers.

claim: The reduction in extracellular acetylcholine reflects abnormal cholinergic neurotransmission in vivo in Dlx-CKO mice
source: To test if the alteration of cholinergic markers reflected abnormal cholinergic neurotransmission in vivo, we performed striatal microdialysis in awake, behaving mice (Song et al., 2012).
evidence: This is the interpretation of the microdialysis findings.

claim: The cholinergic abnormalities in Dlx-CKO mice reflect loss of large cholinergic interneurons
source: To determine if cholinergic abnormalities in Dlx-CKO mice reflect loss of LCIs, we quantified the number of LCIs in control and Dlx-CKO mice at 10 weeks of age, after all abnormal behaviors are fully established.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested, supported by subsequent stereological data.

claim: The striatum can be subdivided into discrete circuits based on anatomical organization
source: To explore whether LCIs might be lost from a specific striatal sub-region reflecting a discrete circuit (Alexander et al., 1986), we subdivided the dorsal striatum into four quadrants and examined cell density throughout its rostro-caudal extent (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is implied by the experimental design and citation to Alexander et al., 1986.

claim: Cell loss in Dlx-CKO striatum does not appear to be selective for patch or matrix striatal subregions
source: Cell loss did not appear to be selective for the patch or matrix striatal subregions.
evidence: This is an observational finding from the anatomical analysis.

claim: Postnatal conditional deletion of Tor1a in cholinergic neurons does not cause overt abnormal movements
source: In contrast to our findings using the Dlx5/6-Cre transgene, which is active prior to these events (in progenitor cells), postnatal conditional deletion of Tor1a in cholinergic neurons does not cause overt abnormal movements or changes in striatal LCI number, morphology, and neurochemistry (Sciamanna et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sciamanna et al., 2012a.

claim: Postnatal conditional deletion of Tor1a in cholinergic neurons does not cause changes in striatal LCI number, morphology, and neurochemistry
source: In contrast to our findings using the Dlx5/6-Cre transgene, which is active prior to these events (in progenitor cells), postnatal conditional deletion of Tor1a in cholinergic neurons does not cause overt abnormal movements or changes in striatal LCI number, morphology, and neurochemistry (Sciamanna et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sciamanna et al., 2012a.

claim: Timing of torsinA deletion plays an important role in disease pathophysiology
source: Consistent with an important role for timing of deletion, germline heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice exhibit increased LCI cell body area, though these mutants show no difference in the number of LCIs (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing different models with different timing of torsinA loss, supported by citation.

claim: Germline heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice exhibit increased LCI cell body area
source: Consistent with an important role for timing of deletion, germline heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice exhibit increased LCI cell body area, though these mutants show no difference in the number of LCIs (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2013.

claim: Germline heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice show no difference in the number of LCIs
source: Consistent with an important role for timing of deletion, germline heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice exhibit increased LCI cell body area, though these mutants show no difference in the number of LCIs (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2013.

claim: Heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice retain considerable torsinA function
source: Mice may require more marked torsinA loss of function to fully model cholinergic vulnerability, as the heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice retain considerable torsinA function, and do not exhibit overt abnormal movements (Tanabe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation, supported by citation.

claim: Heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice do not exhibit overt abnormal movements
source: Mice may require more marked torsinA loss of function to fully model cholinergic vulnerability, as the heterozygous ΔE Tor1a knock-in mice retain considerable torsinA function, and do not exhibit overt abnormal movements (Tanabe et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tanabe et al., 2012.

claim: Conditional deletion of torsinA in medium spiny neurons does not cause overt abnormal movements
source: However, conditional deletion of torsinA in MSNs, which constitute 95% of all striatal neurons, does not cause overt abnormal movements (Yokoi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yokoi et al., 2011.

claim: Medium spiny neurons constitute 95% of all striatal neurons
source: However, conditional deletion of torsinA in MSNs, which constitute 95% of all striatal neurons, does not cause overt abnormal movements (Yokoi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Current dogma holds that neurodegeneration does not occur in primary dystonia
source: Current dogma holds that neurodegeneration does not occur in primary dystonia, but postmortem samples from DYT1 subjects are limited and have not been assessed quantitatively for abnormalities in the number of striatal neuronal cell types (Paudel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as current dogma in the field, with citation.

claim: Postmortem samples from DYT1 subjects have not been assessed quantitatively for abnormalities in the number of striatal neuronal cell types
source: Current dogma holds that neurodegeneration does not occur in primary dystonia, but postmortem samples from DYT1 subjects are limited and have not been assessed quantitatively for abnormalities in the number of striatal neuronal cell types (Paudel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature, with citation.

claim: Neuroimaging studies increasingly point to changes potentially consistent with cell loss in primary dystonia
source: Neuroimaging studies increasingly point to changes potentially consistent with cell loss (reviewed in Ramdhani and Simonyan (2013)).
evidence: Supported by review citation to Ramdhani and Simonyan (2013).

claim: The analysis of postmortem tissue from DYT1 subjects is the first to examine cell type-specific markers in striatum in this context
source: Our studies in postmortem striatum from DYT1 subjects, the first to examine cell type-specific markers in this context, are consistent with our experimental findings pointing to selective cholinergic defect in this structure.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the current work.

claim: Overtly symptomatic DYT1 models demonstrate loss of neurons of the deep cerebellar nuclei with preservation of all other cerebellar cell types
source: Previous work in overtly symptomatic DYT1 models demonstrates loss of discrete cell types in other motor-related structures (e.g., loss of neurons of the deep cerebellar nuclei, with preservation of all other cerebellar cell types (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2014.

claim: Postmortem analyses of DYT1 subjects suggest the presence of inclusion bodies in pedunculopontine cholinergic neurons
source: Postmortem analyses of DYT1 subjects suggests the presence of inclusion bodies in pedunculopontine cholinergic neurons, but did not report cell loss (McNaught et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to McNaught et al., 2004.

claim: Postmortem analyses of DYT1 subjects did not report cell loss in pedunculopontine cholinergic neurons
source: Postmortem analyses of DYT1 subjects suggests the presence of inclusion bodies in pedunculopontine cholinergic neurons, but did not report cell loss (McNaught et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to McNaught et al., 2004.

claim: Abnormal protein quality control may represent a pathogenic event in DYT1 dystonia
source: These observations, and additional work (Liang et al., 2014) and reviewed by Dauer (2014), suggest that abnormal protein quality control may represent a pathogenic event in DYT1 dystonia.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from multiple observations, supported by citations.

claim: Unilateral immunotoxin-mediated striatal cholinergic ablation causes asymmetric concaving postures in mice
source: Unilateral immunotoxin-mediated striatal cholinergic ablation causes 'asymmetric concaving postures' in mice (Kaneko et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaneko et al., 2000.

claim: Large cholinergic interneuron ablation reduces the threshold for the development of motor tics
source: and LCI ablation also reduces the threshold for the development of motor tics (Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Large cholinergic interneurons are lost in a perinatal hypoxia-ischemia model of cerebral palsy-associated dystonia
source: LCIs are lost in a perinatal hypoxia-ischemia model of cerebral palsy-associated dystonia, mimicking the striatal pathology seen in that disease ('status marmoratus') (Burke and Karanas, 1990)
evidence: Supported by citation to Burke and Karanas, 1990.

claim: Cerebral palsy-associated dystonia is treated with anticholinergic drugs
source: LCIs are lost in a perinatal hypoxia-ischemia model of cerebral palsy-associated dystonia, mimicking the striatal pathology seen in that disease ('status marmoratus') (Burke and Karanas, 1990), which is also treated with anticholinergic drugs.
evidence: This is stated as established clinical knowledge, with citation providing context.

claim: Imaging studies of idiopathic cervical dystonia subjects suggest deficits in the density of striatal cholinergic axon terminals
source: Furthermore, imaging studies of idiopathic cervical dystonia subjects suggest deficits in the density of striatal cholinergic axon terminals (Albin et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albin et al., 2003.

claim: Large cholinergic interneurons innervate fast-spiking interneurons
source: LCIs innervate fast-spiking interneurons (Koos and Tepper, 2002), a cell type concentrated in the lateral striatal areas (Berke, 2011) where LCI loss is greatest in Dlx-CKO mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Koos and Tepper, 2002.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons are concentrated in the lateral striatal areas
source: LCIs innervate fast-spiking interneurons (Koos and Tepper, 2002), a cell type concentrated in the lateral striatal areas (Berke, 2011) where LCI loss is greatest in Dlx-CKO mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to Berke, 2011.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons contribute to action execution and suppression of unwanted movements
source: Fast-spiking interneurons contribute to action execution and suppression of unwanted movements (Gage et al., 2010), and have been implicated in dystonic-like postures (Gittis et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gage et al., 2010.

claim: Fast-spiking interneurons have been implicated in dystonic-like postures
source: Fast-spiking interneurons contribute to action execution and suppression of unwanted movements (Gage et al., 2010), and have been implicated in dystonic-like postures (Gittis et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gittis et al., 2011.

claim: Previous reports of DYT1 rodent models support a role between torsinA loss of function and aberrant physiological properties of large cholinergic interneurons
source: Previous reports of DYT1 rodent models support a role between torsinA loss of function and aberrant physiological properties of LCIs (Eskow Jaunarajs et al., 2015), but these models do not exhibit abnormal twisting movements or cell loss (Sharma et al., 2005; Pisani et al., 2006; Martella et al., 2009; Quartarone and Pisani, 2011; Sciamanna et al., 2011, 2012b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Previous DYT1 rodent models with aberrant LCI physiology do not exhibit abnormal twisting movements or cell loss
source: Previous reports of DYT1 rodent models support a role between torsinA loss of function and aberrant physiological properties of LCIs (Eskow Jaunarajs et al., 2015), but these models do not exhibit abnormal twisting movements or cell loss (Sharma et al., 2005; Pisani et al., 2006; Martella et al., 2009; Quartarone and Pisani, 2011; Sciamanna et al., 2011, 2012b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Abnormal clasping is present in a transgenic rat model of dystonia
source: Abnormal clasping is present in a transgenic rat model of dystonia, but it is not known if striatal LCI number is reduced in these animals (Grundmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grundmann et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of cholinergic neurons may be required for the remaining cells to become interconnected into an abnormal circuit
source: Loss of cholinergic neurons may be required for the remaining cells to become interconnected into an abnormal circuit.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The beneficial effect of anticholinergic agents may in part arise from suppressing aberrant large cholinergic interneuron signaling
source: These multiple disturbances of surviving LCIs function raise the possibility that the beneficial effect of anticholinergic agents may in part arise from suppressing their aberrant signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Large cholinergic interneurons are the first striatal neurons to become post-mitotic
source: LCIs are the first striatal neurons to become post-mitotic (Phelps et al., 1989), and cholinergic signaling is believed to have important but poorly understood influences on the development of later-born striatal neurons (Chesselet et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Phelps et al., 1989.

claim: Cholinergic signaling is believed to have important but poorly understood influences on the development of later-born striatal neurons
source: LCIs are the first striatal neurons to become post-mitotic (Phelps et al., 1989), and cholinergic signaling is believed to have important but poorly understood influences on the development of later-born striatal neurons (Chesselet et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chesselet et al., 2007.

claim: Subjects that carry the DYT1 mutation but do not manifest dystonia by their mid-20's almost invariably remain asymptomatic for life
source: Subjects that carry the DYT1 mutation but do not manifest dystonia by their mid-20's almost invariably remain asymptomatic for life (Bressman et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bressman et al., 2000.

claim: TorsinA deficiency during a defined developmental window is a key component of DYT1 pathogenesis
source: These clinical and experimental observations support a critical role for torsinA during CNS maturation, and suggest that torsinA deficiency during a defined developmental window is a key component of DYT1 pathogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and clinical observations.

claim: Previous torsinA loss-of-function models demonstrate cell loss restricted to a neurodevelopmental window
source: Previous torsinA loss-of-function models also demonstrate cell loss restricted to a neurodevelopmental window (Liang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liang et al., 2014.

claim: CNS maturation, synaptogenesis, and associated processes may exert a unique stress on neuronal circuits
source: These observations suggest that CNS maturation, synaptogenesis, and associated processes may exert a unique stress on neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: TorsinA has putative functions in protein quality control
source: TorsinA is a AAA+ protein chaperone (Ozelius et al., 1997) with putative functions in protein quality control (Chen et al., 2010; Nery et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2010 and Nery et al., 2011.

claim: TorsinA has putative functions in regulation of nucleocytoskeletal connections
source: regulation of nucleocytoskeletal connections (Gerace, 2004; Worman and Gundersen, 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerace, 2004 and Worman and Gundersen, 2006.

claim: TorsinA has putative functions in trafficking of membrane-bound proteins
source: trafficking of membrane-bound proteins (Torres et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Torres et al., 2004.

claim: TorsinA has putative functions in protein secretion
source: protein secretion (Hewett et al., 2007, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hewett et al., 2007, 2008.

claim: TorsinA has putative functions in nuclear export of large ribonucleoprotein granules during synapse development
source: and nuclear export of large ribonucleoprotein granules during synapse development (Jokhi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jokhi et al., 2013.

claim: Periods of synaptogenesis and circuit maturation are periods in which torsinA function may be particularly important
source: Periods of synaptogenesis and circuit maturation are therefore periods in which torsinA function may be particularly important.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the putative functions of torsinA and the timing of cell loss.

claim: Cell loss and behavior onset during a neurodevelopmental window is consistent with a critical period for torsinA function in CNS development
source: Cell loss and behavior onset during a neurodevelopmental window is consistent with a critical period for torsinA function in CNS development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal correlation of cell loss and behavior onset.

claim: Unique classes of striatal large cholinergic interneurons may exist that vary in their molecular and functional features
source: These experiments also raise the possibility that unique classes of striatal LCIs may exist that vary in their molecular and functional features.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the selective vulnerability observed.

claim: Dlx-CKO mice exhibit stance width differences compared to controls
source: Genotype differences were present in stance width (two-way ANOVA main effect of genotype F1,62 = 16.51, p < 0.0001; limb F1,62 = 70.90, p < 0.0001; Interaction F1,62 = 0.381, p = 0.539, Sidak's multiple comparisons test), but no other abnormalities were observed.
evidence: Supported by gait analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
